_doc: The living half of the KAZE-KIRI-007 page. The card's address is burned into a chip and can never change, so this page is the only place depth can accumulate: someone who taps the card again next month should find something that was not here today. Adding an entry is a JSON edit and a deploy — never a new page and never a new URL. Newest first. Every number here is on the page above, or is arithmetic on numbers that are, or is measured from the supplied files by a command anyone holding them can re-run. What has never happened is a measurement off a built object, because nobody has built one.

entries.en: The lock is 2 mm too big for the hole it goes through
entries.body_en: The page said the tab slides into a 0.46 mm slot. The cutting file has no such feature: the tab is 10 mm where it leaves the sheet and the notch is 8 mm.
entries._audit_body_en: The spec row and build step 5 both carried the package's numbers — 'LOCK 3 wedge tabs, 0.15 mm clearance, slot 0.46 mm' and 'the material is 0.26 mm and the slot is 0.46 mm, so the tab goes in by hand'. Measured 2026-08-16 against examples/kaze-card/assets/KAZE-KIRI-007_1to1.svg, identical for all three pairs: tab 'M 439.822971502571 10 L 451.822971502571 8 L 451.822971502571 22 L 439.822971502571 20' spans y 10 to 20 at the sheet edge, so 10.0 mm at the root, flaring to 14.0 mm at the tip; notch 'M 0 11 L 10 11 L 10 19 L 0 19' is an 8.0 mm opening 10 mm deep. The string 0.46 does not occur in that SVG at all, and 0.15 occurs once, as prose inside a <text> label rather than as geometry. The lock is three open notches in the left edge, not slits, so the comparison that matters is tab root against notch opening, and the tab is 2 mm too tall. WHERE THE 0.46 ACTUALLY COMES FROM, and it is the more useful half: examples/kaze-card/package/index.html lines 423-424 compute 'var tabClearance = 0.15' and 'var slotWidth = t + 0.2', which is 0.46 at t = 0.26, and lines 433-434 emit both into the spec table. Nothing in the drawing ever reads them. So this is not a mistyped number: it is one generator producing a spec table and a cut file that were never checked against each other — the same shape as the ruler on the card reading four times out while the SVG's own rulers were exact. Both places on the page are corrected and step 5 now sends the reader to scrap first, because this is the one error here that costs a whole sheet. Adjacent and unresolved: the hinge row says 0.3 mm of material is left on a 0.26 mm sheet, which cannot be a remaining depth, and the docs never say whether it means a bridge width instead. Independently re-measured off the same files by a second session before publication.

entries.en: The air slits take off a fifth of a percent, not eight
entries.body_en: The package says the twelve slits cut the weight by 8%. Measured in the cutting file they remove 72 square millimetres out of 37,385, which is 0.19%.
entries._audit_body_en: package/index.html line 268 states the golden-angle vents 'reduce weight 8% and let it close flat'. Measured 2026-08-16 against examples/kaze-card/assets/KAZE-KIRI-007_1to1.svg: the twelve vent paths in the cut group each bound to exactly 6.0 by 2.0 mm and are closed four-point rhombi, so each is 0.5 x 6 x 2 = 6 mm2 and twelve are 72 mm2. The sheet rectangle in that group is width 439.822971502571 by height 85 = 37,385 mm2. 72/37385 = 0.193%. Read them the other way, as full 6 by 2 rectangles, and it is 144/37385 = 0.385% — so the 8% claim is wrong under either reading, which is worth stating because the obvious objection is that the rhombus was measured wrong. The 8% figure appears nowhere else with any working behind it. The spacing half of the same sentence survives and is exact: every vent centre equals (i x 167.988) mod 439.823, largest deviation across all twelve 0.0005 mm, and 167.988 mm along the strip is 137.5 degrees round a 140 mm ring. One further thing the arithmetic surfaced: the first vent is centred on x = 0.0 with a half-width of 3 mm, so half of it falls outside the sheet and the remainder overlaps the second notch at x 0-3, y 38.5-39.98. Eleven whole vents and one broken one. Neither weight nor airflow has been measured on an object, because none exists. Independently re-measured by a second session before publication.

entries.en: The 38 degrees was copied off the wrong line
entries.body_en: This card says its 38° twist was inherited from card 005. Card 005's twist is 22.5°; its 38° is how far it opens from flat, which is a different measurement.
entries._audit_body_en: AUTHORSHIP.md line 8 records the human selection as 'twist 38 deg to inherit from Aurelia Corona 38 deg'. src/site/aurelia/index.html lines 391-392 carry the two angles as adjacent rows of one table: TWIST, '22.5 deg between the bottom rim and the top rim'; and OPENS TO, '38 deg from flat — the drawing's figure, never measured'. Read at source 2026-08-16. The quantity inherited is therefore card 005's opening angle, used here as a twist angle. This does not make 38 degrees a bad choice for this collar; it makes the reason given for it wrong, and the reason is the whole basis of the compounding claim the book runs on. Two knock-ons, and both cite examples/kaze-card/package/index.html rather than the SVG, because that is where the solver lives — the cutting file is 18 paths and carries no script at all. First, package/index.html line 420 computes 'var offset = b * Math.tan(twist*Math.PI/180) * 0.2', which is 5.727 mm at 38 degrees, while the shipped 1:1 SVG uses a fixed 8.0 mm slant on every unit; 8.0 would need 47.5 degrees. So KAZE-KIRI-007_1to1.svg is not what pressing 'Download clean cut paths' produces, and the drawings on this page are traced from the file rather than from the solver. Second, the card prints a collapse of 85 mm to 12 mm, 7.08:1, while package/index.html line 422 computes 'var collapseRatio = H / (N*t*0.8 + 2)' = 85/4.496 = 18.906, a collapsed height of 4.5 mm. Neither has been measured. Independently re-measured by a second session before publication.

entries.en: The ruler on the card was four times out
entries.body_en: The card printed a ruler marked 0 to 20 mm that actually measured 79.5 mm. A ruler that lies is worse than none, so it was replaced with a true 40 mm bar.
entries._audit_body_en: The card arrived with a calibration scale labelled 0–20 mm. Measured against the card's own trim width — 85.6 mm across, a fixed and checkable dimension — that scale spanned 79.5 mm of card. It was out by a factor of just under four. A scale bar has exactly one job: it proves the print came out at true size, so anyone checking their printer against this one would have concluded a correct print was 75% too small, or trusted a print that was four times off. That is worse than shipping no ruler at all, because a missing ruler tells you to go and find one. It is now a true 40 mm bar with ticks at 0, 10, 20, 30 and 40, and it is the second step of the build instructions on this page for that reason. Measure the artefact. Do not trust the number printed beside it.

entries.en: Two proofing guides would have printed on the card
entries.body_en: The artwork carried a dashed trim rectangle and a dotted safe-zone rectangle inside the face. Both were drawn to be looked at, not printed, and both would have printed, so both were removed.
entries._audit_body_en: Two guide rectangles sat inside the card face: a dashed one marking the trim line and a dotted one marking the safe zone that type has to stay inside. Guides like these are for the person laying the card out. They are not part of the design, and anything inside the face is printed — there is no layer that the printer skips. So the finished card would have carried two rectangles of dotted ink across the artwork, which on a two-colour card is not a small blemish. The package's own kill log names this failure and says guides live outside the face or not at all, which means the rule was written down and the artwork still shipped with them. Both were removed before anything was printed. The general form: a mark made to be looked at during the work is a mark that has to be deleted before the work is finished.

entries.en: The first package to declare its own tap-mark colour and be right
entries.body_en: Card 007 wrote down how pale the patch under the chip is: 224 out of 255. Measured on the finished front artwork, the same patch came out at 221.
entries._audit_body_en: The chip sits behind a small patch of the front face, and that patch is left as flat washi with no stripes across it so the tap mark printed on top of it stays readable. How dark to print that mark depends on how pale the patch is, and this is the first package in the book that declared the answer rather than leaving it to be worked out: 224 out of 255, mean brightness, with the patch given in millimetres. Measured back off the finished front artwork, the same rectangle comes out at 221 of 255 — a difference of three parts in 255, which is a little over one percent and well inside the slop of measuring a rectangle whose edges are given to a tenth of a millimetre. A declared number that survives an independent measurement is rarer in this book than it should be. Three of the six cards before this one shipped a code pointing at a domain that does not exist. This one wrote a number down and the number held.
